questions.body: What is the formal mathematical distinction between Big-O, Big-Ω (Omega), and Big-Θ (Theta) notations?
questions.keyPoints: Big-O is asymptotic upper bound; Big-Omega is asymptotic lower bound; Big-Theta is tight bound (both upper and lower).

options.text: Big-O is asymptotic upper bound `(f(n) <= c*g(n))`; Big-Ω is asymptotic lower bound `(f(n) >= c*g(n))`; Big-Θ is tight bound (both upper and lower).
options.explanation: Big-O describes worst-case upper ceilings. Big-Omega describes minimum lower performance floors. Big-Theta describes tight asymptotic bounds where upper and lower growth rates coincide.

options.text: Big-O is best case; Big-Ω is average case; Big-Θ is worst case.
options.explanation: Common misconception: best/average/worst are scenarios; O/Ω/Θ are mathematical bounds applicable to any scenario.

options.text: Big-O measures CPU instructions; Big-Ω measures memory allocations.
options.explanation: All three can be applied to measure time, memory, network calls, or any growth metric.

options.text: Big-Θ only applies to algorithms running on quantum computers.
options.explanation: Big-Theta is standard classical asymptotic notation.

questions.body: What is the difference between 'Auxiliary Space' and 'Total Space Complexity' of an algorithm?
questions.keyPoints: Auxiliary space is temporary space allocated by the algorithm excluding input size; total space includes input size.

options.text: Auxiliary Space measures temporary/extra memory allocated by the algorithm during execution; Total Space includes both auxiliary space AND the memory consumed by the input data.
options.explanation: When comparing sorting algorithms, MergeSort requires O(N) auxiliary space (extra buffer), while HeapSort requires O(1) auxiliary space (in-place), even though both operate on an O(N) input array.

options.text: Auxiliary space is hard drive swap space; total space is RAM.
options.explanation: Both measure RAM allocated in virtual memory.

options.text: Total space only counts stack frames, while auxiliary space counts heap memory.
options.explanation: Both stack frames and heap allocations count toward auxiliary space.

options.text: There is no difference; they are exact synonyms.
options.explanation: Distinguishing input size from algorithm-allocated overhead is critical in complexity analysis.

questions.body: What is the auxiliary space complexity of a recursive function that calculates Fibonacci numbers with maximum recursion tree depth of N?
questions.keyPoints: O(N) space due to maximum call stack depth.

options.text: O(N) space, because the call stack holds at most N stack frames simultaneously along the deepest recursion branch.
options.explanation: Even though naive recursive Fibonacci takes exponential O(2^N) time, the call stack unwinds between branches, so the maximum memory used at any single point in time is proportional to maximum tree depth O(N).
Stack frames are deallocated as calls return; memory does not equal total function calls.
Each recursive invocation allocates a new activation record (stack frame) on the thread call stack.
Linear recursion chains reach depth N, not log N.

questions.body:
What is the time complexity of the following nested loop?
```python
for i in range(n):
    j = 1
    while j < n:
        j *= 2
```
questions.keyPoints: Outer loop runs N times; inner loop runs log2(N) times -> O(N log N).

options.explanation: The outer loop executes `N` times. The inner loop doubles `j` each time (`1, 2, 4, 8, ...`), executing `log2(N)` times per outer iteration. Total operations = `N * log2(N) = O(N log N)`.
The inner loop does not increment by 1; it doubles geometrically.
The inner loop runs multiple times per outer step.
The outer loop runs N times, multiplying the inner cost.

questions.body:
What is the time complexity of the following loop structure?
```python
i = n
while i > 0:
    for j in range(i):
        pass
    i //= 2
```

options.explanation: The total operations sum: `N + N/2 + N/4 + N/8 + ... + 1`. This is a decreasing geometric series with common ratio 1/2, whose sum is bounded by `N / (1 - 1/2) = 2N = O(N)`.
While there are log N iterations of the outer loop, the inner loop work halves each time, summing to O(N).
The sum is strictly bounded by 2N, far less than N^2.
The first iteration alone does N operations.

questions.body: What are the average-case and worst-case time complexities for lookup in a Hash Table?
questions.keyPoints: Average: O(1); Worst-case: O(N) when all keys hash to the same bucket (hash collision).

options.text: Average: O(1), Worst-case: O(N) (when severe hash collisions force traversal of a long linked list or bucket).
options.explanation: With a good hash function and proper load factor, distribution is uniform and lookup is O(1) average. If all keys collide into the same bucket, lookup degrades to O(N) (or O(log N) in Java 8+ HashMap red-black tree bins).

options.text: Average: O(log N), Worst-case: O(log N)
options.explanation: O(log N) applies to balanced binary search trees (e.g. `std::map`, `TreeMap`).
Collision degradation prevents strictly O(1) worst-case without perfect static hashing.
Hash tables provide constant average time.

questions.body: In modern versions of Java (Java 7u6+) and Python, what is the space complexity of creating a substring of length K (`s.substring(start, start + K)`)?
questions.keyPoints: O(K) auxiliary space because a new char array is copied, avoiding memory retention leaks of parent strings.

options.text: O(K) auxiliary space, because modern runtimes copy the characters into a new independent memory buffer.
options.explanation: Legacy Java used shared underlying char arrays with offsets (O(1) memory), which caused massive memory leaks when tiny substrings kept huge parent strings alive. Modern runtimes allocate new copies of size O(K).

options.text: O(1) space, because strings always share the parent pointer.
options.explanation: That legacy implementation was abandoned to prevent memory retention leaks.

options.text: O(N) where N is the original string length.
options.explanation: Only K characters are copied into the new buffer.
Strings store characters linearly in memory.

questions.body: What are the time complexities for `peek`, `insert` (push), and `extractMin` (pop) in a Binary Min-Heap of size N?
questions.keyPoints: peek: O(1), insert: O(log N), extractMin: O(log N).

options.explanation: The root element is always the minimum (peek = O(1)). Inserting appends at the bottom and bubbles up (O(log N)). Extracting swaps the root with the last leaf and bubbles down (O(log N)).
The root is directly accessible at index 0 in O(1).
Restoring heap invariants requires logarithmic bubble up/down steps.
Heaps are tree structures with logarithmic depth.

questions.body: Why does building a binary heap from an unsorted array of N elements using the bottom-up `heapify` algorithm take O(N) time instead of O(N log N)?
questions.keyPoints: Most nodes sit near the bottom of the tree where the bubble-down distance is small; the mathematical sum converges to O(N).

options.text: Most nodes reside at or near the bottom leaves where bubble-down distance is minimal (e.g. N/2 leaves take 0 swaps); the sum of `(h * N / 2^h)` converges to `O(N)`.
options.explanation: Inserting elements one-by-one is O(N log N). But bottom-up heapify runs `siftDown` starting at `N/2` down to `0`. Half the nodes take 0 steps, a quarter take 1 step, etc., forming a series that converges strictly to O(N).

options.text: Because it uses parallel multithreading on modern CPUs.
options.explanation: It is an asymptotic mathematical property of the sequential algorithm.

options.text: Because the array is pre-sorted before heapifying.
options.explanation: Heapify operates on completely unsorted arbitrary arrays.

options.text: Because binary search is applied to find leaf positions.
options.explanation: Heap indices are computed directly via 2*i + 1 and 2*i + 2.

questions.body: Which case of the Master Theorem describes Strassen's matrix multiplication algorithm `T(N) = 7T(N/2) + O(N^2)`?

options.text: Case 1: `a > b^d` (`7 > 2^2`), so work is dominated by the subproblems at the leaves, giving `T(N) = O(N^(log2(7))) ≈ O(N^2.807)`.
options.explanation: Here `a = 7`, `b = 2`, `d = 2`. `log2(7) ≈ 2.807`. Since `2.807 > 2`, leaf work dominates, giving `O(N^2.807)`, improving over naive `O(N^3)` matrix multiplication.

options.text: Case 2: `a == b^d`, yielding O(N^2 log N).
options.explanation: `7 != 4`, so Case 2 does not apply.
`7 > 4`, not less than.

options.text: The Master Theorem cannot be applied to Strassen's algorithm.
options.explanation: Strassen's recurrence fits the Master Theorem polynomial definition perfectly.

questions.body: What is the formal definition of an 'In-Place' algorithm regarding auxiliary space complexity?
questions.keyPoints: An algorithm that transforms input using O(1) auxiliary space (or O(log N) for call stack in QuickSort).

questions.body:
What is the time complexity of the following loop used for primality testing?
```python
i = 2
while i * i <= n:
    if n % i == 0:
        return False
    i += 1
return True
```
questions.keyPoints: O(sqrt(N)) time because the loop terminates when i > sqrt(N).

options.explanation: The condition `i * i <= n` is equivalent to `i <= √n`. Incrementing `i` by 1 on each step means the loop runs at most `√n - 1` times, achieving `O(√N)` time.
Testing all integers up to N is O(N); stopping at `i * i <= n` reduces it to O(√N).
`i` increments by 1, not multiplied by 2.
The loop runs sub-linearly.
